A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same COG research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original interpolation and centroid experiments, generative subspace examples, inversion-budget analyses and Gaussian simulations.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds normality-test comparisons and quantitative analyses linking latent validity to reconstruction and interpolation quality.

M1.justification: COG's affine correction (v1 Equation 3; v2 Equation 4), interpolation weights and subspace construction remain unchanged. v2 Section 3 adds an auxiliary procedure for diagnosing seed-latent validity using normality tests, particularly Kolmogorov-Smirnov. This does not establish that the retained COG benchmark pipeline incorporated filtering.

E1.justification: ImageNet1k images and ShapeNet point clouds remain the real-data coverage. v2 Appendix D extends the synthetic latent-input scenarios beyond v1's mode and constant-vector examples to ramps, scaling, shifts, duplicated coordinates and sparse coordinate rescaling. The chair and point-cloud examples moved into the main text already existed in v1.

E2.justification: The interpolation and centroid comparator sets remain unchanged. However, v2 Table 2 introduces a substantial diagnostic comparison: Kolmogorov-Smirnov is evaluated alongside Shapiro-Wilk, chi-square, Cramér–von Mises, Gaussian likelihood and norm likelihood. The newly discussed Zheng et al. interpolation method is not experimentally benchmarked.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a 200-image normality/reconstruction study, a broader inversion-budget sweep, a 0.001 acceptance threshold, LPIPS reconstruction measurements and Q-Align evaluation of central spherical interpolants. The existing 400-step COG benchmark remains. Separately, Section 5.1 rewrites the mode-norm target as sqrt(D), while Appendix E retains v1's square-root-of-chi-square-mode definition; this inconsistent description does not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: v1 already illustrated inversion-budget failures and the insufficiency of likely norms. v2 substantially extends these analyses with systematic diagnostic comparisons, acceptance versus reconstruction quality, and seed normality versus interpolant quality (Figures 4–5 and Appendix D). These investigate additional failure mechanisms rather than merely redisplaying the earlier examples.

E5.justification: v1 reports 99% intervals from 10,000 Gaussian draws in Appendix B. v2 retains these and adds normality-test p-values, 0.1%–99.9% percentile ranges over 10,000 samples in stochastic test cases, and reported 50%/95% intervals around reconstruction and quality summaries. No increase in repeated runs of the retained COG benchmark is established.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the matched appendix benchmark tables retain their scores, including COG interpolation accuracy 67.4% and FID 38.9. v2 adds extensive diagnostic outcomes: Table 2 reports, for example, p=0 for Kolmogorov-Smirnov versus p=1 for Shapiro-Wilk on the zero-vector case. Figures 4–5 add acceptance, LPIPS and Q-Align results linking seed normality to generation quality.

T1.justification: The five lemmas and their proofs in Appendices A–C remain substantively unchanged. Section 3.1 adds a mathematical reduction asserting equivalent standard-normal testing after z=Σ^(-1)(x−µ). This is new mathematical reasoning, but the stated transformation does not whiten a general covariance matrix; the reported unit-covariance examples avoid that particular problem.

C1.justification: v2 retains the original claims about general, model-agnostic COG combinations and adds a central contribution: normality tests can diagnose unsuitable interpolation seeds even when they reconstruct images well. This becomes an explicit introduction contribution and a recommendation in the conclusion, substantially broadening the paper's contribution beyond COG itself.

C2.justification: v2 develops the interpretation of inversion failures through normality diagnostics and newly acknowledges that standard tests may not capture the characteristics required by a network. Appendix D also interprets differences among tests. Its claim that Cramér–von Mises separates every failure case at the specified percentiles overstates Table 2: the duplicated-coordinate upper value, 7e-4, exceeds the real-sample lower value, 2e-4.

D1.justification: v2 documents diagnostic implementation choices, including 30 histogram bins for chi-square and explicit coordinate-perturbation constructions in Appendix D/Table 2. Appendix B newly specifies v=0.5 for the existing beta-interval calculation. The main inversion, guidance, grouping and classifier settings remain documented as before.

R1.justification: New background and related-work sections substantially expand positioning against non-Gaussian-prior approaches, conditional generation and latent editing methods. Added discussions include Fadel, Davidson, Park's pullback metric and Zheng's interpolation approach, alongside classical normality-testing literature. The Haas preprint-to-publication update itself is not a new research comparison.

P1.justification: The introduction is extensively rewritten around explicit contributions, and the document gains dedicated Background, Normality Assessment, Related Work and Conclusion sections. Existing methodology and experiments are reorganized, and v1's appendix discussion of atypical high-likelihood vectors is integrated into the main narrative. The title, author ordering and affiliations also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds diagnostic Figures 4–5 and the colored normality-comparison Table 2. v1 Figure 11 is condensed and rearranged into v2 Figure 3, while the existing rocking-chair and point-cloud figures move into the main text as Figures 6–7. Typography, running headers, captions and figure placement are extensively revised.

improvement.justification: v2 turns v1's qualitative warning about invalid inversion seeds into a concrete, quantitatively evaluated diagnostic, substantially improving practical assessment of a key assumption (Section 3, Figures 4–5, Appendix D). Expanded background and research positioning also clarify applicability. The covariance-normalization error and overstated Cramér–von Mises separation claim need correction, but are localized and do not invalidate the reported unit-Gaussian Kolmogorov-Smirnov evidence. The improvement comes from stronger diagnostic support and explanation, not improved COG benchmark scores.
